PROP
4
REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 4
YES ON PROPOSITION 4, THE CALIFORNIA FAIR ELECTIONS ACT: ELECTIONS SHOULD BE WON, NOT BOUGHT
The amount of money in California elections is outrageous; it's distorting our democracy. Since 2020, more than $1 billion has been spent on California state candidate races alone. This massive spending gives special interests greater access and influence while drowning out the voices of ordinary Californians.
PROP. 4 HELPS QUALIFIED CANDIDATES COMPETE
Running for office today often requires either personal wealth or access to wealthy donors. Deep pockets have become an unofficial requirement to run for office, leaving too many qualified candidates behind.
PROP. 4 CHANGES THE WAY WE FINANCE ELECTION CAMPAIGNS
Programs like small-dollar donation matching help candidates compete without relying on wealthy donors. However, most California communities are banned from using these tools, allowing the influence of big money to grow.
Proposition 4 lifts that ban, giving voters and local governments the option to adopt public financing with strict safeguards so qualified candidates-regardless of their income-can compete against candidates who are backed by wealthy interests.
PROP. 4 BUILDS ON A PROVEN MODEL
We know this reform works because it's working in other states. Thousands of candidates from different backgrounds have been elected in fourteen states and 26 localities using similar systems. They are new people with good ideas from all walks of life. Because they don't rely on wealthy donors, they can speak their mind and work for the people, not the special interests.
PROP. 4 GIVES LOCAL COMMUNITIES A CHOICE
Proposition 4 does not create a public financing program. It simply gives local governments the option to adopt one if they choose.
If a community does, the cost is as little as $1 per resident each year-a small investment to help counter the billions spent influencing California's elections.
PROP. 4 PROTECTS TAXPAYERS
Taxpayer Safeguards:
Requires candidates to meet strict eligibility criteria and abide by spending limits to qualify for public funds.
Prohibits public funding from favoring incumbents or discriminating based on political party.
Prohibits the use of public funds for legal defense or fines.
PROP. 4 CRACKS DOWN ON ILLEGAL FOREIGN MONEY
Proposition 4 triples the maximum fines for illegal foreign campaign contributions and expenditures, strengthening penalties for those who attempt to interfere in California's elections.
PROP. 4 IS SUPPORTED BY LEADERS ACROSS CALIFORNIA
Proposition 4 is backed by a broad coalition including League of Women Voters of California, California Nurses Association, Mental Health Advocacy Services, Social Security Works, California Clean Money Campaign, California Common Cause, California National Organization for Women, Californians for Disability Rights, Consumer Watchdog, Courage California, Democracy for America, Indivisible California: Statestrong, La Defensa, Money Out Voters In, Voters Right to Know, and many others.
PROP. 4 GIVES CALIFORNIANS THE OPPORTUNITY TO RECLAIM THEIR ELECTIONS and ensure they reflect the values of the people, not just the wealthiest donors.
YES ON 4-Restore power to voters, not wealthy donors
Lorrel Plimier , Co-President
League of Women Voters of California
Catherine Kennedy , President
California Nurses Association
Tom Umberg , California State Senator
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 4
Here is what the politicians supporting Proposition 4 do not tell you:
Proposition 4 REPEALS the voter-approved law that PROHIBITS candidates from using taxpayer money to run for office.
Proposition 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money. In the election last June, more than 60 candidates ran for Governor. Proposition 4 would allow thousands of candidates to get taxpayer money!
Proposition 4 has NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money a candidate can get. Proposition 4 opens the door to taxpayer-funded campaigns but provides no limits on how much taxpayer money a candidate can get and NO LIMIT on spending. It will lead to more negative ads, more junk mail, and more annoying text messages.
Proposition 4 does NOT PROHIBIT SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY in campaigns. Proposition 4 ALLOWS candidates to get taxpayer money AND to get special interest money! Where exactly is the money going to come from to fund thousands of political campaigns? Proposition 4 does not say. But you know the answer. It is coming from YOU, the taxpayers! Less money for schools, less money for public safety, less money for healthcare. More money for politicians.
Proposition 4 is a BLANK CHECK. It is based on false promises and failed solutions.
Proposition 4 does NOT protect taxpayers. That is why Proposition 4 is opposed by California's leading taxpayer organizations.
Proposition 4 does NOT provide for “fair elections.” That is why Proposition 4 is opposed by former Commissioners of the Fair Political Practices Commission.
Vote NO ON PROPOSITION 4.
Robert Gutierrez , President
California Taxpayers Association
Jon Coupal , President
Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association
Dan Schnur , Former Chair
Fair Political Practices Commission
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 4
Why did Sacramento politicians put Proposition 4 on the ballot? They want access to YOUR TAXPAYER MONEY to fund THEIR OWN CAMPAIGNS.
Proposition 4 repeals a voter approved law that PROHIBITS these politicians from using public taxpayer funds for their own campaigns. That's right, Proposition 4 allows politicians to use your taxpayer money to fund their campaigns.
Proposition 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money and NO LIMIT on how much money they can get! Proposition 4 is a BLANK CHECK. There isn't even a limit on how much they can spend on their campaigns! More negative ads. More junk mail. More annoying text messages. More, more, more.
Proposition 4 is so poorly written, it could allow every state or local “candidate” to get public funding. They don't even have to actually qualify for the ballot to get taxpayer money. Proposition 4 allows for public funding of thousands of state and local candidates. It even allows for public financing of candidates for county political party committees.
In just the last primary election, there were more than 60 candidates for Governor. Do you want YOUR TAXPAYER MONEY going to support more of their negative campaign ads and junk mail?
Proposition 4 has NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money a candidate can receive. It says it requires “strict criteria” to receive taxpayer funds but provides NO DETAILS on what the criteria are! Read the fine print:
“‘Strict criteria' means the requirement set by statute, ordinance, or charter that candidates must meet to receive public funds.”
But there is no current statute, ordinance or charter setting any criteria. Guess who will be setting the criteria? The same politicians who want to get your taxpayer money!
Some good government groups support public financing of campaigns because they want to get special interest money out of politics. BUT PROPOSITION 4 DOES NOT GET RID OF SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY! Under Proposition 4, candidates can raise money from special interests AND get public funding too.
Proposition 4 is the worst kind of public financing scheme. It provides no specifics. It leaves all the details to be worked out by the same politicians who want to get access to public funds.
It is a blank check. But worse than that, Proposition 4 allows special-interest funding of political campaigns.
Please join California's leading taxpayer protection organizations, including the California Taxpayers Association, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California, United Latinos Action, as well as former members of California's Fair Political Practices Commission, who all oppose Proposition 4.
PLEASE VOTE NO ON THE POLITICIANS' BLANK CHECK PROPOSITION. VOTE NO ON PROP. 4.
Dan Schnur , Former Chair
Fair Political Practices Commission
Colleen McAndrews , Former Commissioner
Fair Political Practices Commission
Julian Canete , President
California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 4
DON'T BE MISLED BY SPECIAL INTERESTS WHO WANT TO KEEP BUYING ELECTIONS
California is the ONLY state that bans public funding of campaigns. Communities in all 49 other states have the right to adopt public financing to allow qualified candidates to compete against wealthy donors. California doesn't. Prop. 4 simply removes that ban and gives local voters the same choice everyone else has, while instituting strict taxpayer safeguards.
PROP. 4 GIVES POWER BACK TO LOCAL COMMUNITIES AND EMPOWERS VOTERS, NOT DONORS
Prop. 4 doesn't spend a single taxpayer dollar or institute public financing anywhere. It simply removes the ban to give every city, county, and the state the right to adopt public funding if local voters want it. The details are appropriately left to each community. But any system MUST require candidates to abide by spending limits and demonstrate broad-based support in their district to qualify.
PROP. 4 MAKES ELECTED OFFICIALS ACCOUNTABLE TO VOTERS, NOT DONORS
Corporate special interests oppose Prop. 4 because public financing allows candidates to run and win without relying on them-threatening their grip on California elections.
Thousands of candidates from different backgrounds have been elected across the country using public financing, for a tiny cost. Because they don't rely on wealthy donors, they can speak their minds and work for the people, not special interests.
DON'T BE FOOLED BY CORPORATE SPECIAL INTERESTS HIDING BEHIND NICE-SOUNDING NAMES.
VOTE YES ON 4 to let local voters and communities reclaim their elections so they're won, not bought.
Carmen Balber , Executive Director
Consumer Watchdog
Camerina Davidson , President
California National Organization for Women
Darius Kemp , Executive Director
California Common Cause

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Forty-two percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 55 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 43 percent said they would vote yes and 51 percent would vote no. Proposition 4: Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding
Proposition 4: Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding
Proposition 4: Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns. Legislative Statute.
Additional Titles
Public Fundraising, Allow Public Financing of Election Campaigns Measure
Summary
Proposition 4 was placed on the ballot by Senate Bill 42 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) (SB 42). SB 42 changes provisions of the Political Reform Act of 1974, which bans the use of public funds for candidates’ political campaigns. The senate passed the bill in June 2025, with the Assembly passing it in September 2025. Gov. Gavin Newsom signed the bill in October, sending it to the ballot as Proposition 4.
Proposition 4 would remove California’s prohibition on using public money to finance political candidates, allowing state and local governments to establish publicly funded campaign programs in the future. The measure would not itself create such a program, but would give governments the option to develop their own systems within statewide guidelines.
Under the measure, funds dedicated to purposes such as education, transportation, and public safety could not be redirected to campaigns. Candidates receiving public financing would have to demonstrate a sufficient level of support among voters and comply with spending limits and other program requirements. Public funds could not be used for legal defense costs, fines, or repayment of a candidate’s personal campaign loans. State and local governments would determine the details of their individual programs, while the Fair Political Practices Commission (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/) could provide guidance on complying with Proposition 4 but would not be required to administer or enforce local programs.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 4 would not automatically require new spending because it does not establish a public campaign financing program. Costs would arise only if the state or local governments later choose to create such programs, with the amount depending on how widely they are adopted and how they are structured. The state would also likely spend a few hundred thousand dollars annually for additional Fair Political Practices Commission (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/) staff to advise governments on developing programs that comply with the measure.
What your vote means
Yes: A “yes” vote would end the statewide ban on public campaign financing, allowing state and local governments to establish programs that provide public funds to qualifying candidates under specified rules and spending limits.
No: A “no” vote would maintain the existing prohibition on public financing of campaigns, including the current exception for certain charter cities.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that Proposition 4 would reduce the influence of wealthy donors and special interests by allowing state and local governments to establish public campaign financing programs. They say these programs could help qualified candidates compete for office without relying heavily on wealthy donors, while requiring participating candidates to meet eligibility requirements and spending limits. Proposition 4 would also prohibit using funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety and would strengthen penalties for illegal foreign campaign contributions.
Opponents argue that Proposition 4 could allow taxpayer money to be used to fund political campaigns without setting specific limits on how much public funding candidates could receive. They contend that important details are not included, leaving many key decisions to future state and local decision makers. Critics note that candidates receiving public funds could still accept private and special-interest contributions, meaning the measure would not eliminate private money from campaigns.

In summary
Prop. 4 would lift a ban that prohibits state and most local candidates from using public funding for their political campaigns. Proponents argue the mechanism helps more candidates run for office, but opponents are skeptical.
Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called.
In 1988, a Democrat, a Republican and an independent in the state Legislature co-authored a ballot measure to ban most political campaigns from using public money.
Their rationale? There was already too much money in politics.
“It certainly makes no sense to open the biggest money source of all, the taxpayers’ purses and wallets,” proponents argued (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1988&context=ca_ballot_props). Nearly 60% of voters agreed.
Almost four decades later, some good-government groups argue that the state needs to do the exact opposite to counter the influence of money in politics.
They, along with the state Democratic Party, are backing Proposition 4 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-4-public-fundraising/) on the November ballot, which would lift the 1988 ban and authorize the state and most local governments to set up public campaign financing systems for state and local races.
Seven charter cities in California, including San Francisco, Berkeley and Oakland, were spared from the 1988 ban and already have public campaign financing.
To qualify for the funding, candidates must meet criteria such as proving they have a certain number of small donors or agreeing to cap how much they raise and spend on their campaign. Depending on the city, eligible candidates receive the funding as a grant, a matching fund indexed to their total donations, or a voucher voters can give to campaigns.
Proponents of Prop. 4 may face an uphill battle: Voters have twice rejected similar ballot measures to lift the ban, and public polling so far suggests voters are skeptical.
What supporters, opponents say
Elections have gotten more expensive over the past three decades, both federally and statewide.
In 2000, federal candidates, parties and special interests spent $5.6 billion on congressional and presidential races. By 2020, that number had nearly quadrupled to $18 billion (https://www.opensecrets.org/elections-overview/cost-of-election?display=T), according to OpenSecrets, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit that tracks campaign spending nationwide.
In California, special interests spent $26 million (https://calmatters.org/politics/2025/10/prop50-money-ads-mailers-billboards/) running competing ads on redistricting last year, making it the most expensive ballot measure race in state history. This year, California had the most expensive governor’s race (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/03/us/elections/california-governor-campaign-finance.html) in U.S. history, with billionaire Tom Steyer pouring $213 million (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-rich-candidates-funding-elections/) of his own money into his unsuccessful gubernatorial bid.
Supporters of Prop. 4 say public campaign financing is necessary as a check against that kind of unfettered private campaign spending, because candidates often must accept campaign spending limits to qualify for public funding. They say public financing will lead to more diverse candidates by attracting those who otherwise couldn’t afford to run for office.

“We need to change the way we finance election campaigns so candidates can run and win without having to raise big money, and they can spend their time listening to voters rather than their donors,” said Trent Lange, president of California Clean Money Campaign and co-chair of the Yes on Prop. 4 campaign.
Gov. Gavin Newsom (https://calmatters.org/tag/gavin-newsom/) and the Democratic-led state Legislature, which voted last year (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb42) to place Prop. 4 on the November ballot, also support the measure. Sen. Tom Umberg (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/thomas-umberg-165043), a Santa Ana Democrat and a co-author of Prop. 4, said it would help alleviate a “growing cynicism in politics” and allow candidates to spend more time developing policies instead of fundraising.
“To the extent that we can engage particularly small donors, that will … empower and also engage the body politic, particularly young people,” he said.
But opponents say politicians should not use taxpayer dollars (https://caltax.org/prop4/) to run campaigns. They argue the measure would force voters to subsidize candidates they otherwise wouldn’t support, and that fraudulent candidates could exploit the system.
Voters have previously rejected ballot initiatives that would have allowed public money to be used for political campaigns. Nearly two-thirds of voters shot down a 2000 measure that would have allowed candidates to tap public funds for advertising (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2000/25_03_2000.html). In 2010, 58% of voters opposed a 2010 measure (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_15,_Biennial_Lobbyist_Fee_and_Public_Campaign_Funding_Measure_(June_2010)) to lift the 1988 ban.
“The voters have been quite clear they don’t want taxpayer money being used for politics,” Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican, said last year (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/278290#t=221&f=fe479f37ee7a3df6888379e9be069fd8) on the Assembly floor. “Unfortunately, politicians simply can’t take no for an answer.”

Critics also doubt the effectiveness of Prop. 4, arguing it is not specific enough to have teeth.
Prop. 4 offers only broad instructions to local governments and the state. It would ban candidates from using public funds meant for education, public safety and transportation. It would require candidates to prove they have enough public support and to agree to certain spending limits to receive funding, but doesn’t spell out how much. It would also ban candidates from using the money to pay for legal defenses, fines or personal loans to their campaigns.
The measure specifically exempts the Fair Political Practices Commission, the state’s campaign finance watchdog, from ensuring local programs are not exploited or abused, leaving it largely to local governments. But not every local government has its own watchdog agency, let alone an effective one.
The San Francisco Chronicle’s editorial board, in opposing Prop. 4, argued that its rules “are only meaningful if they’re enforced by independent, nonpartisan bodies. And Prop. 4 offers no guarantee they will be.”
Effectiveness debate
Fifteen states and Washington, D.C., offer some sort of statewide public financing for political campaigns, according to an analysis by the National Conference of State Legislatures (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/public-financing-of-campaigns-overview).
Studies are mixed on the effectiveness of those programs.
Some, including one in 2003 (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1532673X03256784) by two University of Maryland scholars, suggest that candidates who accept public financing spend less time fundraising, freeing them up for other campaign activities.
Some researchers found that public financing expanded the pool of candidates running for office. A 2022 study of Seattle’s program (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0047272722000780), which gives each registered voter four $25 vouchers to contribute to the campaign of their choice, concluded that the program boosted the number of candidates by 86%. Another study (https://web.stanford.edu/~neilm/The%20Impact%20of%20Public%20Financing%20on%20Electoral%20Competition.pdf) of Arizona and Maine’s programs found that they “significantly increased competition.”
Others disagreed. The United States Government Accountability Office, the nonpartisan research agency advising Congress, studied Arizona and Maine’s programs (https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-10-390.pdf) in 2010 and concluded there was no evidence that public financing led to more candidates.
There’s little evidence that public financing has curbed the influence of private donors, according to the Seattle study and the GAO report.
In California, few studies have examined the effectiveness of local programs. A 2023 San Francisco Ethics Commission study found candidates have increasingly tapped into the public funds and that third-party spending was “at near all-time lows.” But the commission encouraged a more comprehensive analysis. A 2013 study (https://www.oaklandca.gov/files/assets/city/v/3/boards-amp-commissions/documents/pec/publications/reports-by-third-parties/2013-05-01-evaluating-oaklands-limited-public-financing-act.pdf) in Oakland found no evidence its program diluted the influence of wealthy donors, although it did seem to boost competition.
Researchers point to the difficulty (https://sgp.jhu.edu/primers/public-funding-of-us-elections/#conclusion) of studying public financing programs, because most apply in only a handful of states and it is hard to measure what would have happened if the programs had not been in place.
The lack of compelling evidence makes Prop. 4 proponents’ claims shaky, the San Diego Union-Tribune’s editorial board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/09/04/endorsement-dont-buy-prop-4s-baloney-about-publicly-financed-campaigns/) argued.
“So Proposition 4’s only certain effect would be to create a new category of government spending that taxpayers could be required to pay for — one with no track record of delivering promised benefits,” it said.
The ballot measure should not be overly prescriptive, said Dora Rose, deputy director for the League of Women Voters of California, a co-sponsor of Prop. 4.
“Prop. 4 sets basic safeguards and then lets communities learn from the evidence and decide what works for them,” she said.
For now, voters appear skeptical. A September poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the Public Policy Institute of California found 53% of likely voters would oppose Prop. 4, while just 42% would vote yes. Another poll (https://escholarship.org/content/qt3w14s99c/qt3w14s99c.pdf) by the UC-Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies shows a tighter matchup, with 35% of likely voters supporting the measure and another 35% against it.

Proposition 4
Allow public financing of political campaigns
This would authorize California’s state and local governments to establish public campaign funds for candidates if they choose to. It would reverse a 1988 ban on such systems for the state and most local governments. Currently, only five California cities have public financing for local offices, including Berkeley and San Francisco. The California Legislature put this measure on the ballot.
Weigh the arguments.
Take our quizzes to learn more about each proposition.
BEGIN → (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/quizzes)
Support
Oppose
Summary
Support
Advocates say public campaign financing helps curb the influence of private money in politics. They argue that public financing encourages candidates without significant financial backing to run and empowers small donors.
Oppose
Opponents say the measure would force taxpayers to subsidize political candidates they may not want to support and could direct funding to fraudulent candidates. They argue that it is also expensive for state and local governments to establish the system.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).

Outside spending
Separate from proposition committees, outside groups can pay for ads, mailers and other efforts to influence voters. They can’t coordinate that spending with proposition committees. There is no limit on how much they can spend.

REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE. Repeals prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns. Public funding programs may not use funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety. Fiscal Impact: Ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public campaign finance programs.

Table Coding Key
Y = Yes, the group endorses the measure.
N = No, the group does not endorse the measure.
NP = Group stated NO POSITION or NEUTRAL
- [dash] = endorsement could not be located
NOTE: a blank box means the source has not yet been checked and verified.
Endorsements checked and updated as of November 2, 2026.

Proposition 4
November 3, 2026, General Election
Proposition 4
Taxpayer-Funded Political Campaigns
RECOMMENDATION: VOTE NO ON PROPOSITION 4
The California Taxpayers Association recommends a “no” vote on Proposition 4 because it would remove California’s constitutional prohibition on the use of taxpayer dollars to finance political campaigns. Eliminating this safeguard would pave the way for politicians to spend our tax dollars on campaign junk mail, including negative mailers, endless television ads, and other political communications. Californians’ tax dollars should be used to fund essential public services – not political campaigns.
PROVISIONS
Program Authorization
Authorizes Politicians to Use Tax Dollars for Political Campaigns. Proposition 4 authorizes the state and local governments to establish public campaign financing programs – the use of tax dollars to pay for political ads and other campaigning – through statute, ordinance, or charter. This would effectively remove the statewide ban established by the Political Reform Act of 1974 and the improvements to the act that were overwhelmingly approved by voters in 1988.
Allows Use of Tax Dollars to Fund Extremist Candidates and Campaign Hit Pieces. Any program created to use tax dollars for political campaigning must be neutral, prohibiting distinctions based on a candidate’s political party, their status as a challenger or incumbent, or their campaign messaging – effectively forcing taxpayers to pay for the campaigns of candidates with whom they may fundamentally disagree, and allowing the use of tax dollars to produce annoying negative ads, extremist messages, hate-based campaigning, and other advertising that many taxpayers would find abhorrent.
Allows “Candidates” to Receive Tax Dollars Even if They Don’t Appear on the Ballot. Proposition 4 could allow every state or local “candidate” to receive taxpayer dollars, even if they don’t actually qualify for the ballot. A person becomes a “candidate” under campaign finance law when they file a notice of intent to be a candidate and start raising money, which typically happens long before a person becomes a “candidate” on the ballot by filing nomination papers. (For example, most major candidates for governor in California’s 2026 primary began raising money in 2025 or earlier, but didn’t file nomination papers until shortly before the March 2026 deadline.)
New Systems Not Enforceable by the Fair Political Practices Commission. Proposition 4 states that the Fair Political Practices Commission (FPPC) – the agency responsible for administering California’s campaign finance laws and enforcing the Political Reform Act – would not be responsible for implementing and enforcing the new system of taxpayer-funded political campaigns.
No Limit on Number of Candidates Who Would Receive Tax Dollars for Campaigning. Proposition 4 has no limit on the number of candidates who could get taxpayer money for their campaigns.
Expansion Beyond Charter Cities. Public financing programs currently operate in some charter cities. Proposition 4 expands this authority so that all local governments, including more than 3,000 special districts, may establish public financing systems that would apply to all candidates regardless of political affiliation.
Incumbents Receive Tax Dollars. While Proposition 4 ostensibly is intended to make it easier for people of all walks of life to run for public office, it would allow incumbent politicians – who typically begin any campaign with a major advantage – to receive tax dollars for their campaigns. For example, in the 2026 race in Los Angeles – one of the charter cities that already has a taxpayer-financed campaign system – incumbent Mayor Karen Bass and City Council Member Nithya Raman each received more than $1.2 million in tax dollars for their campaigns.
Authorizes Use of Tax Dollars to Fund Races for County Political Party Committees. Proposition 4 allows tax dollars to be used to pay for the campaigns of candidates for county political party committees, effectively forcing taxpayers to pay for a political party’s internal activities even if they have fundamental disagreements with the party or are not members of any political party.
Lacks Provisions to Curtail Special-Interest Funding of Campaigns. Proposition 4 does not stop special-interest funding of campaigns. Candidates could raise money from special interests, benefit from independent expenditures, and additionally get tax dollars to fund their campaigns.
Funding
Earmarked Funds Prohibited. Public money earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety could not be used to fund election campaigns under Proposition 4, but the measure does not establish a funding mechanism and allows state and local governments to determine funding sources, essentially allowing them to shortchange other core government services by using tax dollars for political campaigns instead of services that benefit the community.
Prohibited Uses of Public Funds. Public funds could not be directly used to pay for legal defense fees or fines. Candidates who receive public financing are permanently prohibited from repaying personal loans from any source after the campaign.
Candidate Contribution and Spending
Broad-Based Voter Requirement. Proposition 4 states that candidates must meet “strict criteria” to demonstrate the extent of their support, but does not define this term or establish the criteria.
$10 Contribution Limit. Proposition 4 states that when a program uses contributions to determine eligibility for receiving tax dollars for campaigning, only the first $10 of any contribution may be counted toward that requirement.
Adjustment for Independent Expenditures . Voluntary expenditure limits must be set by the state and local governments before funds are issued. However, local governments can increase a candidate’s spending cap using a “net supportive funds” formula that accounts for independent expenditures supporting or opposing all candidates in the race (Net Supportive Funds = [Available Candidate Funds + IEs in Support] – IEs in Opposition).
Foreign Contributions
Increased Penalties for Foreign Contributions. Proposition 4 maintains the existing prohibitions on contributions, expenditures, or independent expenditures made by foreign governments, foreign principals, and foreign nationals in state or local elections, or ballot measure campaigns. However, penalties would increase from the current “equal to the amount contributed” standard to up to three times the illegal contribution or expenditure.
FISCAL IMPACT
Proposition 4 generated a one-time state cost to be placed on the November 2026 ballot and creates ongoing state administrative costs for the FPPC, estimated at more than $198,000 annually. The FPPC also notes that it potentially could incur significant additional enforcement costs. The measure would create potentially significant and unpredictable local government costs for any jurisdiction that chooses to adopt a system of taxpayer-funded campaigns. Proposition 4 provides no additional information as to how a public financing program should be organized and administered; therefore, local costs would vary widely depending on factors such as program design and staffing capacity. Additionally, the measure does not prohibit future state appropriations for the purpose of public financing, meaning a future Legislature could decide to put state tax dollars toward these programs.
BACKGROUND
Statewide Ban on Public Campaign Financing. In 1988, voters approved Proposition 73 (1988), which amended the Political Reform Act of 1974 and prohibited public officers and candidates from accepting public funds for campaign purposes. However, the California Supreme Court ruled in Johnson v. Bradley (1992) that the ban does not apply to charter cities, allowing them to create local public financing systems.
Past Public Financing Ballot Measures. California voters rejected two previous attempts to repeal the public financing ban: Proposition 25 (2000) and Proposition 15 (2010).
Past Public Financing Legislation. SB 1107, signed into law in 2016, attempted to authorize public financing statewide, but the Third District Court of Appeal ruled in Howard Jarvis Association v. Newsom (2019) that such changes must be approved by voters, since Proposition 73 amended the Political Reform Act.
POLICY CONSIDERATIONS
How Much Tax Money Will Be Used for Political Campaigns Instead of Services for Taxpayers? By removing the legal barrier preventing state and local governments from using tax dollars for political campaigns, Proposition 4 opens the door for the Legislature and local governments to allocate taxpayer dollars toward campaign financing. Because the measure does not establish funding limits, structures, or safeguards, it creates uncertainty about the scale of future public expenditures. While no funding is mandated under Proposition 4 itself, its passage could enable the development of statewide or local systems funded through general tax revenue or newly created funding streams. It would also require additional administrative oversight and program costs, adding to government spending at a time when the state faces a budget deficit.
Diverting Public Funds for Campaigns. Proposition 4 prohibits education, transportation, and public safety funding from being redirected to public financing programs, but this would not preclude cities or counties from redirecting existing funds to create a public financing program. The measure also would allow public financing programs to be created by redirecting funding from the following special districts: airports, cemeteries, electric utilities, emergency medical services, flood control, garbage, harbor/port operations, healthcare, libraries, mosquito/vector control, parks and recreation, open space, and water.
FPPC Oversight Gap. Proposition 4 states that the FPPC is not responsible for administering or enforcing local public financing programs. However, the FPPC would retain authority over statewide campaign finance laws and is expected to incur ongoing costs to provide regulatory guidance and address related enforcement issues. Therefore, local public finance structures not under the oversight of the FPPC could be vulnerable to inconsistent enforcement and fraudulent practices.
Many Types of Office Holders May be Eligible for Public Financing. Proposition 4 provides public financing for potentially many different types of office holders in California, including:
Governor
Lieutenant Governor
Attorney General
Secretary of State
State Controller
State Treasurer
Insurance Commissioner
Superintendent of Public Instruction
State Board of Equalization Member

Public Confidence and Trust in Elections. Proposition 4 would authorize the spending of tax dollars to support candidates whom some taxpayers strongly oppose. Although courts have upheld properly structured voluntary public financing systems, such programs create concerns about public confidence in government and elections. In an era when many voters across the political spectrum already distrust political institutions and election administration, directing public funds to candidates could be viewed by some as government financing politicians, favoring insiders, or using taxpayer money for politics rather than core public services. Even if administered fairly, the perception of self-dealing or partisan advantage could deepen skepticism and further erode trust in democratic institutions. Because Proposition 4 cannot prohibit independent expenditures, public funds may supplement rather than replace private campaign spending, potentially increasing the overall amount of money in politics while raising questions about whether the system is achieving its intended reform goals.

Peter is the Vice President of Policy at CalTax. He has been with CalTax since 2011, first as a Policy Analyst and since 2015 as a registered lobbyist. In addition to representing CalTax in the Capitol, he analyzes legislation relating to tax policy, and manages special projects. He also provides research and writing for CalTax publications. Peter’s research and writing covers a broad spectrum of state tax policy, as well as government efficiency, elections and local tax issues. He is a graduate of the University of San Diego.

David Kline
David was named Vice President of Communications and Research in January 2010, after serving since 2007 as Director of Communications. He fields media inquiries, oversees research projects and production of CalTax publications, and serves as editor of the CalTaxletter . The findings mark a significant decline in support of the measure, which was crafted by an influential California healthcare union to compensate for an estimated $100 billion in federal healthcare cuts approved by President Trump and congressional Republicans.

Nearly $368 million has been contributed to efforts opposing the billionaire tax, while $36 million has been donated to support the proposed levy.
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of billionaires who resided in California as of Jan. 1, with some exceptions. Democrats and their allies are splintered over the proposal. Some, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, argue it will prompt the wealthy to flee California, further harming its volatile budget, which is dependent on the state’s richest residents. The California Democratic Party and leading progressives support the measure, with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) calling it a modest tax necessary to help Californians struggling because of cuts imposed by Republicans to pay for tax breaks for the wealthy.
While Republican voters overwhelmingly oppose Proposition 40, nearly two-thirds of Democrats support it and more than a quarter opposing it. There is also a generational divide, with 6 out of 10 voters 65 years old or older opposing the measure, while more than two-thirds of those under 30 supporting it, according to the poll.
The findings are similar to a Public Policy Institute of California poll released Tuesday, which found 52% of likely voters would vote against Proposition 40, while 46% supported it.
The campaign against the wealth tax, funded by some of California’s richest tech moguls, is centered on three intertwined ballot initiatives: Proposition 40 and Propositions 41 and 42, both of which would undercut Proposition 40 through a series of changes to state tax laws and spending restrictions.

## Proposition 4: Allows public financing of election campaigns
Proposition 4 would repeal California's ban on state and local governments providing public funding for political campaigns.
If approved, local governments could create their own public campaign financing programs, subject to restrictions on the use of public money.
Funds earmarked for education, transportation and public safety could not be used for those programs.
A yes vote would allow state and local governments to create qualifying public financing programs.
A no vote would leave the existing ban in place.
Supporters including the League of Women Voters of California and the California Nurses Association say the measure could limit the power and influence of private funding in elections.
Opponents, which include the California Taxpayers Association and the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, argue that public money should not be used to finance political campaigns.

Another notable finding was voters’ support of Proposition 3, which would make permanent a higher income tax rate on the wealthy (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-3-high-income-tax-voter-guide) that funds education. A majority of voters — 54% — support continuing the levy, while 37% oppose it, according to the poll. DiCamillo says the disparity in support of the proposed billionaire tax and the extension of the existing wealth tax has been consistent in IGS’s polls, and is likely because of the differing foundations of the levies.
“Proposition 3 is already in place, and if you read the fiscal impact, if this were to pass, it maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual funding,” he said, “It’s a big revenue generator, and I think that is something that’s already in place.”
“Voters kind of understand the progressive nature of California’s tax system, and they kind of support that, but they don’t support nearly as much the idea of some new kind of tax, the wealth tax, which is taxing assets rather than income,” he said. “So that’s the distinction.”
These ballot measures are among 14 that voters will decide (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-07-06/2026-california-propositions-voter-guide-billionaires-tax-voter-id-homebuyers-money-tax-hike-limits) on Nov. 3, as well as statewide, congressional, local and judicial elections.

July 6, 2026
Among the other controversial measures is Proposition 39, a measure pushed by Republicans that would require all voters in future elections to show government-issued identification every time they vote in person or provide a special PIN or the last four digits of their Social Security number when submitting mail-in ballots.
The measure also would require the California secretary of state and county election officials to verify that registered voters are U.S. citizens by “using government data,” which according to supporters could include information in the federal Social Security Administration database, jury summons information and other government records.
Nearly 6 in 10 likely voters oppose the effort, while more than a third support it, split largely along party lines. More than half of voters who are registered as “no party preference” or with a smaller political party oppose the proposal, which DiCamillo said was an indication of trouble for the proposition given the state’s Democratic majority electorate and the proximity of the election.
“It’s hard for Republicans to push something over the finish line by themselves,” he said.
Other prominent ballot measures:
Proposition 43, which would prohibit local governments (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-43-threshold-local-special-tax-voter-guide) from imposing certain new special taxes unless two-thirds of voters approve the proposal. Such proposals need a simple majority vote to be approved. While 46% of likely voters oppose the proposal, 36% support it, challenging numbers this close to election day, DiCamillo said. “It needs to get to 50,” he said. “We’ll see how you do that this late in the campaign.”
Proposition 4, which would repeal a prohibition of public financing of campaigns (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-4-public-campaign-financing-voter-guide), allowing state and local governments to support candidates if they abide by several rules. Likely voters are evenly split about the proposal, with 41% supporting it and opposing it, and 18% undecided. “It’s close, but it’s still below 50%. Most voters tend to vote no in the late going if they’re not convinced,” DiCamillo said, adding that he viewed the lack of support among voters who do not affiliate with a political party as a signal of potential failure.
The poll of 2,787 registered California voters was conducted online in English and Spanish Oct. 19-25 and has a margin of error of about 3 percentage points in either direction.

Methodology Note:
Findings are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents, conducted online using the Ipsos KnowledgePanel. Interviews were conducted in

from October 16—22, 2026.

percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the unweighted sample of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error for unweighted likely voter subgroups
is larger. Sampling error is only one type of error to which surveys are subject. Results may also be affected by factors such as question wording,
question order, and survey timing.

**Evaluating polling data**

I'm looking at a model for strange polls, weighing the prior 74.1% against current data. It’s tricky because there might be conflicting information. The user might want to conduct around 30 checks, so I’m considering getting the latest Berkeley data via an alternative source. I need to evaluate the proposals and tax issues, thinking about whether they're realistic given the past. It seems there are various approaches to this data—some may be hidden or not reflecting the real future.**Forecasting polling outcomes**

I'm analyzing a potential blue wave where Democrats could turn seats to yield around 47.9% or even 49.6% with certain adjustments, but I see challenges in getting above 50% without strong messaging. The forecast seems unrealistic, especially with internal splits among voters regarding tax policies. I wonder if the latest poll shows a tie, which would mean uncertainty. Historical data suggest doubts about outcomes as well. I’ll look for targeted support polling as part of my strategy.

Forecast methodology
How the forecast works
From partisan lean and the national environment to the polling average, candidate effects and 2,000 correlated simulations of the election, county by county.
2,000 simulations Updated November 2, 2026 The forecast (https://www.onpointpolitics.us/forecast)Changelog (https://www.onpointpolitics.us/forecast/changelog)
What the model does
Overview
The forecast rebuilds every 2026 Senate, governor and House race county by county. It starts from what the fundamentals say a race should look like, moves that toward the polling average as the polling gets deeper and the election gets closer, adjusts for the candidates, and then runs the whole election 2,000 times with shared errors so that races move together the way they do on a real election night.
Each race carries three legs. The polling leg takes its statewide level from the polling average and its county shape from each county’s own voting history. The Gallup leg takes each county’s certified 2024 result and moves it by the demographic swing, half of it a county MRP of the On Point Polling national dataset, to the 2026 national environment, alongside the seat’s own past races. The electorate leg is built from Trump’s approval re-estimated in every county from the On Point Polling national dataset, each state at its own level of approval and disapproval with no national flattening, turned into vote with the respondent crosstabs and shaped by the 2026 electorate. Every county’s electorate starts from its citizen adults raked to the state’s 2026 registered voter benchmarks from the voter file. The three are blended into one county forecast, which is then simulated.
Fundamentals
Step 1
Partisan lean. Every state, county and district starts from its presidential lean on the lines in force for 2026, taken from the certified results. On the race pages this is the anchor, the first stage in the breakdown of how the number gets made.
National environment. Every leg is lined up on one national anchor, Democrats ahead by 13.1 points, the On Point Polling final national poll of Oct 28. Behind it sits the full On Point Polling national respondent dataset: all 5,932 respondents in eight waves from February to Oct 28. Where a respondent skipped a question or their wave never asked it, a multilevel regression predicts their answer from their demographics, 2024 vote, party, outlook, approval and turnout history, so every respondent answers every question. The waves are then pooled so later waves count more: opinion is treated as drifting at the rate the 2026 approval average moved, each wave counts by how much it can still say about late October, and no wave falls below a twentieth of its natural share, so every respondent keeps a weight. The Oct 28 poll carries about 59 percent of the pool. The same completed, pooled respondents feed every part of the model that reads respondents: the demographic vote and turnout fits, the state effects, the approval to vote crosstabs, party defection and financial strain. The census leg is also built county by county from an MRP of that dataset: each county’s projected 2026 electorate, from the census, the voter file and the turnout model, joined to its certified 2024 vote, is run through the same cell model, which carries every group shift in the data, Hispanic and rural voters, 2024 vote by area and by race. Half of each county’s census swing from its 2024 result is that county MRP swing. Candidate terms sit outside the swing and are kept whole, Dan Osborn’s 2024 Senate run among them: Nebraska’s approval and census legs carry 61 percent of his county by county margin over the 2024 presidential vote plus his measured personal vote, and his 2024 race leads the seat history. Each state responds to that environment at its own measured rate, built from three measurements, each weighted by how well it is measured and pulled toward the national rate. The first is its presidential swings from 2016 to 2020 and 2020 to 2024 against the nation’s. The second is the On Point Polling state MRP, rebuilt on the completed dataset and measured against a partisan baseline that no longer rests on Trump’s 2024 margin alone: half the state’s 2024 lean, a quarter its 2020 lean and a quarter its 2022 midterm, from how its House vote moved between 2022 and 2024 against the nation’s. The third is a demographic elasticity: the same MRP with every state effect removed, so a state moves only by who lives there and how those groups moved in the database. Hispanic and rural voters moved furthest toward the Democrats there, so Texas now moves about 1.33 times the national swing and Florida about 1.15 times, while Wisconsin, North Carolina, Ohio and Pennsylvania move about 0.73 to 0.79 times. All three are measured on the log odds scale the model applies them on. The 2026 environment also draws on the generic congressional ballot and presidential approval. The generic ballot sets the national vote, and the On Point Polling respondent database supplies approval county by county, calibrated and converted into vote with the On Point Polling respondent crosstabs. Each county responds to the environment through its own elasticity, estimated from a national demographic fit and its own recent presidential swings, so a swing county moves more than a county that votes the same way every cycle.
Incumbency. An incumbent carries a measured personal vote: the county by county gap between that person’s own past races and the nearest presidential race on the same ground. It applies to every sitting governor on the ballot and to none of the open seats. An incumbent who never won the office has no personal vote to carry.
The polling average
Step 2
Every poll of a race enters the average once. A poll’s weight is the product of its sample size, its age, its voter screen, its pollster grade and a penalty for a large undecided share. Recency decays over about three weeks, so a poll fielded a month ago counts for a fraction of one fielded this week. Likely voter samples count three times as much as registered voter samples, and adult samples count very little. Repeated releases from the same pollster inside three weeks are discounted, so one house cannot swamp the average, and any poll more than two standard deviations from the rest is pulled back to that line.
Where a race has 8 or more polls, the level comes from a LOWESS trend instead. Every poll is placed at the midpoint of its field dates, published averages are left out, and a robust LOWESS line is fit at three spans. The Election Day level is 40 percent of the recent trend plus 60 percent of the long term trend, carried flat from the newest poll. That blend missed later polling the least in a backtest of the site’s own polls. The weighted average still supplies the decided share and the third party share, so only the split of the decided vote moves. Races with fewer than 8 polls keep the weighted average.
Pollster grades come from the On Point Polling pollster ratings (https://www.onpointpolitics.us/on-point-polling/methodology), and polls sponsored by a campaign or a party are flagged on every race page. Since Oct 30 those internals are also corrected before they enter the average: every Republican internal is set against the nonpartisan polls other firms ended within three weeks of it in the same race, and every Democratic internal the same way, the gaps are pooled across all races and shrunk by their number, and each internal is moved back by its side’s measured lean. On Oct 30 that was 4.6 points of margin for Republican internals and 2.0 for Democratic ones. Rasmussen Reports is counted, as a Republican internal. Since Oct 31 the same goes for every firm that mainly works for one party, checked against each firm’s own client list and published profiles: Cygnal, Echelon Insights, National Public Affairs, Peak Insights, Remington Research, OnMessage, McLaughlin & Associates, the Tyson Group, Victory Insights, Spry Strategies, Harper Polling, Data Orbital, Data Targeting, Ragnar Research, Deep Root Analytics, Guidant Polling, Susquehanna and co/efficient as Republican, and Patinkin Research, Keating Research, Equis Research, Blueprint and Chism, HIT Strategies and the Maine People’s Resource Center as Democratic. With them in the pools the measured leans are 3.8 points for Republican aligned polls and 1.6 for Democratic aligned ones. Firms whose leaning could not be established, among them Quantus Insights and Big Data Poll, stay unmarked and are weighed on their records. Cygnal no longer counts among the gold standard firms in the national averages.
How polls and fundamentals blend
Step 3
Each race’s weight on its polls is measured, not fixed. The race’s weighted polling average has an error of its own: a floor of 3.5 points of margin that every poll shares, plus 6 points for each poll’s own error, divided by the effective number of polls. That effective count is the Kish count of the average’s own weights, so a few large high quality polls count for more than many small ones, times how fresh the polls are, with a poll keeping half its information four weeks after it closes. The fundamentals carry an error of 7.5 points. The two are combined by precision: the poll weight is 7.5 squared over 7.5 squared plus the poll error squared, held at most at 85 percent.
In practice a race with one fresh poll gives its polls a little over half the weight, a race with four or five effective polls about 70 percent, and the most heavily polled races about 75 percent; a race whose only polls are months old leans almost entirely on its fundamentals. The Gallup leg and the electorate leg split the rest 35 to 20. The early vote no longer moves weight between the legs: it reaches each race through the measured early vote correction after the run.
Candidate effects
Step 4
Beyond incumbency, the model prices the candidates themselves. Party unity comes from each nominee’s share of their own party’s 2026 primary vote, so a nominee who limped out of a divided primary carries less of their party. Each state’s 2026 electorate also reads the parties’ 2026 primary turnout against their 2024 vote, and only real 2026 primary ballots count: a side whose primary was uncontested or has no county results is not stood in for by an older general election, so that state’s electorate comes from its early vote instead. Since Oct 30 the primaries carry far more of each nominee’s county shape. Each nominee’s county share of their own primary moves the county by 0.45 of its gap to their statewide share, up from 0.21, and the groups that voted for them, their home ground and the turnout they drew count 2.5 times the plain reading, up from 1.4. A nominee who ran far behind their statewide share in a county, a distant fourth or fifth there, is hurt more than in proportion: a small shortfall barely changes, a collapse costs several times as much, up to 0.6 log odds in that county. The county primary party split counts at 0.70, up from 0.40, but only the part that the county’s 2024 lean does not already predict. In states where voters can take either party’s ballot, part of a county’s unusual primary turnout is read as crossover from the other party, more when the other party’s own primary was not contested, and it is taken out of both the party split and the nominee’s share. Party unity is unchanged. A nominee who polls behind or ahead of the race’s baseline, the state’s 2024 result moved by the national environment, is read as weaker or stronger by 0.8 of the gap, up to 0.20 log odds. The cap on how far a state can run past its most lopsided past result is softer, with more than twice the room.
Third party and independent candidates are modeled explicitly rather than folded into the major parties. Where an independent is the main challenger, as in Nebraska, that candidate takes the non Republican side of the race and is shown in lavender.
Local conditions, gas, data centers and coalitions
Step 4b
Since Oct 30 half of that census swing, and more, comes from a ground up simulation of every county’s potential voters. The On Point national dataset, all 5,932 respondents with every answer completed, gives each respondent a turnout chance, from their stated intention to vote, their 2022 and 2024 vote history, how many of the people closest to them will vote, whether they already voted and how they plan to vote, and a vote, the leaned generic ballot. Both are fit on 2024 vote by race, college, age, gender and area type, so each county inherits the shift its own 2024 voters made: on the dataset, Hispanic voters are 11.7 points more Democratic than their 2024 vote, rural voters 13.5, voters without a degree 9.1 and Black voters 2.8 points more Republican. How hard each group feels this year’s issues, from the more likely Democrat or Republican questions and approval, nudges its turnout. Every county’s joint table of age, race, college and 2024 vote is raked to its census and voter file marginals, turnout is moved by the reported field programs and the Election Day weather forecast, and the whole electorate is levelled to the Oct 28 national poll, Democrats ahead by 13.1. Then every county is simulated voter by voter, 300 times, each potential voter turning out and voting as their own draw, with national, state, group and county shocks. That simulation sets 65 percent of the census swing and moves each county’s turnout.
Since the night of Oct 30 every simulated voter also has a way of voting, by mail, early in person or on Election Day, and each mode is modeled on its own. The dataset’s ballot method answers give each cell its chance of each mode, and every state’s mix is set to its 2026 target, the state’s 2024 record from the federal Election Administration and Voting Survey pooled with the 2026 answers, as on the early vote page. Each mode gets its own vote, from terms for the mode and for the mode by 2024 vote, shrunk toward zero and centered on the state’s own mix, so they split a cell’s vote among its modes without changing its total; a state where nearly everyone votes by mail does not take on the national mail voters’ selection. The Election Day vote is where the year’s swing shows most: on the dataset, Election Day voters were Trump plus 11.3 in 2024 among the two candidates and are Republican plus 4.3 now, a 6.9 point swing, against 1.7 points by mail and 1.3 early in person. Almost all of that is who votes on Election Day, mostly 2024 Trump voters, who are crossing over at about one in nine whichever way they vote; with 2024 vote and demographics held fixed, the way of voting adds no clear difference of its own, and the model reproduces the Election Day swing from those groups. Weather now falls only on the Election Day voters. Every question in the dataset now counts. Approval, right track, the economy, Iran, the Epstein files, deportation, kept promises, household strain, the 2028 test, ideology, party identification, pro Israel PAC backing and the six message tests feed each group’s intensity, and a voter’s most important issue doubles the message test that speaks to it. How far each 2024 vote by race group can move in the simulation is set by how cross pressured it is: attitudes against its 2024 vote, a party identification that does not match it, undecided before the lean, moderates and the independent and swing political types.
Since Oct 31 the county MRP is its own leg of every Senate and governor forecast, not a sixth of the fundamentals. The leg is half the county MRP and half the ground up simulation, both on the half drift pooled national set and levelled to Democrats ahead by 13.1. The California Fair Elections Act
Vote Yes
Says no to big money in politics
Corporate special interests and billionaires have a near monopoly on funding candidates, corrupting politics and drowning out everyday voters.
Vote Yes
Empowers voters and protects local control
Prop 4 lifts the ban on public funding of campaigns, giving all communities the option to create systems to empower voters and qualified candidates.
Vote Yes
Makes elections about ideas, not money
Public financing helps qualified candidates compete and win, even against corporate special interests and billionaires.
“If the public doesn’t finance political candidates, special interests will happily step in.”
George Skelton, Los Angeles Times, April 2023
Where It Already Works
14 states and 26 local governments across the country have run publicly funded campaigns to empower voters for decades. Five California cities have too.
14
States
26
Local governments
5
California cities
Public funding of campaigns is currently banned everywhere in California except charter cities. General law cities, counties, districts and the state do not have the same right that charter cities have.
Written Into The Measure
Prop 4 does not create a program anywhere. It sets the floor that every program has to clear, so taxpayers are protected wherever one is passed.
No touching money earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety
Candidates must abide by spending limits and meet strict criteria to qualify
No public funds for legal bills, fines, or repaying personal loans
No favoring a party, incumbent, or challenger
Prop 4 also triples the maximum fine for illegal foreign campaign contributions and expenditures, strengthening penalties for those who attempt to interfere in California’s elections.
Who Is Behind Prop 4
Prop 4 is supported by a broad coalition of Californian organizations that fought along with thousands of grassroots supporters over three years to get the legislature to put Prop 4 on the ballot so elections are won, not bought.
